title: Smoke seen from a mile away as army detonates US stockpile of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa
summary:
Controlled blast to dispose of lead azide risks releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in 100-mile radius

The US army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of the the bomb-making material…

blocks.text: The US army detonated the nation’s entire stockpile of the the bomb-making material lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday morning, despite an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects.

The controlled blast, which took place at about 10.00am ET, was to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the chemical that was stored at the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people.
The explosion risked releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed with the weather forecast.

Images taken from a distance away appeared to show a white plume of smoke rising over the town immediately after the blast, before dissipating quickly. One local news station, KWQC, reported seeing a large amount of smoke from more than a mile away.

blocks.caption: Journalists and photographers get set up to document the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa, on 25 November 2026. Photograph: Matthew Putney/EPA

blocks.text: A local reporter in Iowa, who was live on air when the detonation happened, said he heard “a big boom” and and could “actually visibly see the shockwave coming through”.

Others were less impressed by the size of the blast. Tim Brandt, a resident of Burlington, Iowa, told the Associated Press that he wanted to see a big boom and feel the ground shake, but that instead, the detonation reminded him of the noisemakers that crack when thrown on the ground.
“It was nothing,” he said. “It seemed like government put fear in a lot of people over nothing.”
Shortly after the detonation, Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that “early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations”.
Lee Zeldin, head of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), said that he has been told that the blast “caved inward perfectly”.

He said: “When the army was planning its mitigation efforts, there were a number of actions that were taken that included an effort to get the detonation to go… downland and toward unoccupied land within the Iowa army ammunition plant.”
“This message that I just received … First off, the air monitors are showing a remaining zero detection, and as far as the blast itself, it caved inward perfectly.”

The EPA added in a statement that “real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region” and that monitors “never stopped collecting data throughout the event”. The agency also launched a website through which visitors can monitor live air quality readings along the plume route.

blocks.caption: A plume rises after the US army detonated a stockpile of lead azide at its Iowa army ammunition plant. Photograph: Austin Johnson/AP

blocks.text: The acting army secretary, Adam Telle, said that that “the threat of an uncontrolled spontaneous detonation has been eliminated”.

“I am so proud of our SOLDIERS for their courage, training, mitigation and precision! They put it on the line for all of us just like this every day!” he said in a statement. Telle also thanked Trump and his administration “for mobilizing an unprecedented whole of government approach to fix this problem once and for all for the great people of Iowa”.

Lead azide, which typically appears as a white powder or needle-like crystals, is a explosive chemical compound of lead used mainly in detonators, according to the National Center for Biotechnology Information.

The US army said that a routine inspection in March at the Iowa facility found that “decades-old, stored lead azide had partially crystallized, making it increasingly sensitive to friction, shock and cold winter temperatures”.
after newsletter promotion

The army said that the deterioration had “created a new and growing risk of spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation.” The army described lead azide as a “highly sensitive explosive” which becomes “increasingly unstable as it deteriorates”.
Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, has called for “immediate transparency” following the detonation, in order “to understand how and why this situation became what it did”.

blocks.caption: Army personnel and local emergency management officials check in with residents after the detonation. Photograph: Jim Urquhart/Reuters

blocks.text: In a statement on Wednesday, Sand, a Democrat, said that “there is obviously more testing to do that will provide certainty over time, but for now, federal officials have reported that lead dispersal should be limited, Iowans are safe and damage to property is limited.”
Sand also said that he was grateful to the experts on the ground “who did all they could to make this detonation as safe as possible”.
The army released new maps on Tuesday forecasting that the projected path will move south-west of Middletown before extending into northern Missouri.

The army warned: “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.”

After the blast the Federal Emergency Management Agency urged residents in the local area who did not evacuate to shelter in place and continue to follow guidance issued by the EPA and other agencies, and to wait for the all clear to go outside by officials. Fema also said that it has provided safe lodging to those who evacuated.

An emergency notification that was sent to phones on Tuesday said that some people within five miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated and warned those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed to “avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration”. The army encouraged residents who live outside the recommended evacuation zone to shelter in place.
The operation was initially planned for last Friday, but was rescheduled three times as public concern grew and environmentalists sued to block the detonation.
Trump ordered the military to hold off on detonation pending a court ruling and a sign-off from Sand, the Democratic governor-elect, who does not take office until January.

On Monday, a three-judge panel of the eighth circuit court of appeals said the army could proceed with detonating the stockpile, finding that the EPA adequately incorporated safeguards in an emergency permit to minimize the dispersal of dust.
